subtype: Living in fear of the next attack [Actor]
passage: Dear Arohi, You asked why I keep saying no to plans. I owe you the real answer. Since the panic attack on the metro in March, I've been avoiding things. First the metro. Then crowded lectures. Then the big exam hall. I sit near doors. I check where the exits are. I'd rather miss the concert with you than risk it happening in the crowd. But I've started seeing a psychologist, and it's helping. She explained what my body is doing in an attack: my alarm system going off by mistake. My heart speeds up, I breathe too fast, I feel dizzy, and it's scary but not dangerous. Understanding that has taken away half the fear. Last week I did two metro stops with her plan. Next month, maybe the concert? Your friend, Irfan

subtype: Living in fear of the next attack [Actor]
passage: "So, Wasim, since you asked. The first one happened in the university library, and for a year after that I organised my whole life around not having another one. I'm Siddharth. I stopped taking the train home and paid for expensive cabs I couldn't afford. I sat every exam near the door, and I dropped a subject because its exam was in the huge hall. My world shrank to my room, the canteen and one corridor. What changed? My sister made me see a counsellor. She drew me a diagram of what happens: the body's alarm fires, adrenaline, fast heart, fast breathing, the feeling of doom, and then it drops. It always drops. Once I understood that, the attacks lost their power. Now I take the train again, one stop at a time."

subtype: Living in fear of the next attack [Actor]
passage: "Minakshi, you're avoiding the train to college since that bad day? Your Chacha understands. When I was twenty, in Mumbai, I had my first panic on a packed local train at Dadar. Heart like a drum, I thought I would die. After that, I stopped taking trains. I walked two hours to work, every day, in the rain. I stopped going to cinema, to weddings. My world became so small. Finally my mother dragged me to a doctor. He drew a picture of the body's alarm system and said, 'Ramesh, your alarm is ringing when there is no fire.' Then a counsellor helped me practise, one station at a time. It took months. Now look: I ride the trains every day. So tell me, beta, shall we find someone for you to talk to?"

passage: Rehana, twenty, had not entered the big exam hall since last term, when panic struck halfway through her economics paper. This term she had arranged to sit in the small room. Then, ten minutes before the final, a notice went up: all students to the main hall. Her chest tightened at once. "I can't," she told her roommate Binita. Binita stood with her by the noticeboard. "What did your counsellor explain?" Rehana closed her eyes. "The racing heart is just my alarm. It peaks and then it passes. It's not danger." "Then let's walk in together, and sit near the door." Rehana went in. Her heart raced for a while, then settled. She finished the paper.

qa.q: How did understanding her body help Rehana cope?
qa.a: Remembering her counsellor's explanation that the racing heart is an alarm that peaks and passes helped her go in and finish.

qa.a: Binita probably felt supportive and a little anxious for her friend, and glad to see her finish.

subtype: Living in fear of the next attack [Actor]
passage: Last Durga Puja, Anirban, twenty-one, had his first panic attack inside a packed pandal in Kolkata. Since then he had refused every crowded place: no pandals, no metro, no concerts. When this year's Puja came near, he felt sick just hearing the dhak drums. His friend Zainab noticed him cancelling everything. "You've been seeing that psychologist, right? What does she say?" "That my body sounds an alarm with no fire," Anirban said. "And that avoiding keeps the alarm loud." Zainab smiled. "So let's try something small. A quiet neighbourhood pandal, early morning, before the crowds." At seven on Saptami, they stood before the goddess, nearly alone. Anirban's heart raced, then slowed. "I'm here," he said, amazed.

qa.a: They went at seven on Saptami, before the crowds.

qa.a: She may feel happy and proud for him, glad her small idea helped.

"Jomon, the exam hall is that way."
"I know, Leela. I'm taking it in the small room. I told the office I have a headache."
"You did that last month too. And you stopped taking the metro."
Jomon sighed. "Because of what happened in March. What if it happens in the hall? Two hundred people watching me."
"The panic thing?"
"Yes. My heart went crazy, I couldn't breathe, I thought I was dying. Now I'm scared all the time of it coming back."
"That sounds exhausting. Did you ever find out what it was?"
"No."
"My cousin had the same. The counsellor explained it's the body's alarm going off when there's no fire. Knowing that helped her a lot. Come with me to the student wellness centre after this?"
Jomon was quiet. "If I understood it, maybe I wouldn't be so scared of it."
"Exactly. After the exam, then."
